name: Fewest shifts to cover opening hours
brief:
A shop is open from time 0 up to `close`. Each offered shift `[start, end]` covers the time from `start` up to but not including `end`. Choose the fewest shifts that together cover the whole opening, from 0 up to `close`, with no gap. Return that number, or `-1` when the shifts cannot cover it.

Write `fewest_shifts(shifts, close)`.

Example. For `shifts = [[0, 4], [2, 8], [3, 6], [7, 10]]` and `close = 10`, the shifts `[0, 4]`, `[2, 8]` and `[7, 10]` cover it, and no two shifts do, so the answer is 3.
constraints: $1 \le \text{close} \le 10^9$ and $0 \le n \le 200{,}000$, with $\text{start} < \text{end}$, all integers. A shift may start before 0 or end after `close`.
$O(n \log n)$ time is the target. Trying, for each shift, every shift that could follow it is too slow.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Sort by start. With the opening covered up to `reach`, look at every shift that starts at or before `reach` and take the latest end; if no shift moves `reach` forward, there is a gap.

examples.note: Only `[0, 4]` starts the day, `[2, 8]` reaches furthest from there, and `[7, 10]` finishes it.
The second shift starts as the first ends, so there is no gap.
Nobody covers the time from 3 to 4.

tests.call: fewest_shifts([[j * 5, j * 5 + 10] for j in ((i * 7919) % 200000 for i in range(200000))], 1000000)

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Greedy proof: some best cover can take, as its next shift, the one that starts by `reach` and ends latest, because swapping it in covers at least as much.
Picking the longest shift, or the earliest start, is the trap: only how far the next shift reaches matters.
One sort and one pass give $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.
